To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the oxidation of ethanol by brain mitochondria is a significant pathway for the formation of acetaldehydes in the brain, that the acetaldehyde formed is a potent neurotoxin, that the acetylaldehyde formed in the mitochondria is not released into the cytoplasm but is oxidized further to acetate, and that this oxidation of acetaldehyde to acetate by brain mitochondria may be the key to the behavioral effects of ethanol.
ethanol is oxidized to acetaldehyde by a pathway involving alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) in brain, and acetaldehyde is then oxidized to acetic acid by acetaldehyde dehydrogena-se (ALDH).
the oxidation of ethanol is not required for ethanol intoxication and that the metabolism of ethanol to acetoacetate and acetyl CoA, and not acetaldehyde, may be important in ethanol intoxication.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the oxidation of ethanol by the brain and the possible consequences of the production of acetaldehyde.
the role of acetaldehyde as an intermediate in the metabolism of ethanol.
the role of the brain in ethanol metabolism and the possible behavioral and physiological consequences of ethanol oxidation in the brain.

acetaldehyde was not the cause of the intoxication of ethanol.

acetaldehyde is formed in the central nervous systems of animals at concentrations of 10 to 100 μM.
ethanol is oxidized to acetaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase, acetaldehyde dehydrogenases and aldehyde oxidases.
ethanol oxidation to acetaldehyde is not the only pathway of metabolism and acetaldehyde does not appear in the brain in significant amounts following ethanol ingestion.

the oxidation of ethanol is a two-step process.
